ai.literal: Those who possess, that which is called [possession], is zeal; those who do not have that, what they possess, do they possess [it] otherwise?
ai.translation: That which is truly called a possession is one's inner zeal; as for those who lack it, do they really possess whatever else they may own?
ai.modern: ஒருவர் பெற்றுள்ளார் என்று சொல்லத்தக்கது அவரிடம் உள்ள ஊக்கமே ஆகும்; அந்த ஊக்கம் இல்லாதவர்கள் வேறு எதை உடையவராக இருந்தாலும், அவர்கள் எதையும் உடையவர் ஆவார்களோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes that inner energy or zeal (ūkkam) is the only true possession a person can have. The poet argues that if someone lacks this vital drive, any material wealth or other possessions they might hold are of no real value. The rhetorical question "do they really possess?" (uṭaiyarō) highlights that without motivation and willpower, external riches are as good as non-existent. Thus, the chapter on "possession of energy" begins by defining energy itself as the ultimate wealth.

ai.literal: Zeal possession is the true possession; material wealth possession, without staying, departing will go away.
ai.translation: The possession of inner motivation is the only true possession; the possession of material wealth does not last, but will slip away.
ai.modern: ஊக்கத்தை உடைமையாகக் கொண்டிருப்பதே நிலையான உடைமையாகும்; பொருள் உடைமையாக இருப்பது நிலைத்து நிற்காமல் நம்மை விட்டு நீங்கிவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts internal strength with external riches. The word 'uḷḷam' here refers to the inner energy, zeal, or motivation of a person. The poet asserts that having this inner drive is the only permanent and real possession ('uṭaimai') one can own. On the other hand, material wealth ('poruḷ') is transient; it lacks stability and will eventually depart ('nīṅki viṭum') from a person. Therefore, cultivating a motivated mind is far more valuable than gathering material goods.

ai.literal: Wealth we lost saying will not grieve, resolve certainly in hand those who possess.
ai.translation: Those who possess unwavering resolve as a certain asset in hand will not grieve, saying, 'We have lost our wealth.'
ai.modern: ஊக்கத்தை உறுதியான கைப்பொருளாகக் கொண்டவர்கள், 'செல்வத்தை இழந்துவிட்டோமே' என்று வருந்தமாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme value of inner motivation and resolve over material wealth. The poet explains that those who hold onto determination as their secure, permanent possession in hand will never despair when they lose external riches. They understand that material wealth can be lost and regained, but as long as they possess inner drive, they have the ultimate resource to rebuild. Thus, they remain untroubled by temporary setbacks, knowing their true strength lies within.

ai.literal: Prosperity, inquiring the path, will go to the presence of him who has wavering-less energy.
ai.translation: Prosperity will ask for the way and go on its own to the presence of one who possesses unwavering energy.
ai.modern: தளர்ச்சி இல்லாத ஊக்கத்தை உடையவனிடம், செல்வமானது தானே வழியைக் கேட்டுக்கொண்டு போய்ச் சேரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the magnetic power of persistent, unwavering energy (ūkkam). Instead of a person having to struggle and search for wealth, the poet personifies prosperity (ākkam) as an active seeker. Prosperity itself will ask for directions ('atar viṉāy') to find the path that leads directly to the side ('uḻai') of the person who never wavers or gives up ('acaivilā'). The word 'acaivu' here refers to slackness, hesitation, or discouragement, making 'acaivilā' the quality of being steadfast and resolute.

ai.literal: Proportional to the water's depth is the flower's stem length; proportional to their own mind's strength is people's greatness.
ai.translation: The length of a water-lily's stem is proportional to the depth of the water; even so, the height of a person's greatness is proportional to the strength of their inner drive.
ai.modern: நீரின் ஆழத்திற்கு ஏற்ப நீர்வாழ்பூக்களின் தண்டு வளரும்; அதுபோல, மனிதர்களின் ஊக்கத்தின் அளவிற்கு ஏற்ப அவர்களுடைய உயர்வு அமையும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a beautiful natural analogy to explain how inner motivation determines human achievement. The poet points out that the stems of aquatic flowers like lilies grow longer or shorter to match the exact depth of the water they are in. Similarly, the height of a person's greatness is not fixed, but rises in direct proportion to the depth of their determination and enthusiasm. By pairing 'வெள்ளத்து' (of the water) with 'உள்ளத்து' (of the mind), the verse shows that our external success is always a reflection of our internal drive.

ai.literal: All that is thought should be thought of loftily; even if that fails, not failing is its nature.
ai.translation: Let all your thoughts be aimed at greatness; even if you fail to attain it, the very nature of such high aiming is itself a success.
ai.modern: நாம் நினைப்பதையெல்லாம் உயர்ந்ததாகவே நினைக்க வேண்டும்; அந்த எண்ணம் கைகூடாவிட்டாலும், அவ்வாறு நினைப்பதை விடாமல் இருப்பதே பெருமை தருவதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the power of lofty aspirations. The word 'உள்ளுவது' refers to what we think or aim for, and 'உயர்வுள்ளல்' means keeping those thoughts noble and high. Even if circumstances prevent us from achieving that high goal ('தள்ளினும்'), the persistent attitude of aiming high ('தள்ளாமை') possesses the quality ('நீர்த்து') of greatness in itself. It teaches that noble ambition is never a failure, as the effort itself elevates the mind.

parts.gloss: they will not flinch or lose heart

ai.literal: At the time of ruin, they will not flinch, those of strong will, like a war-elephant that, having been pierced by a shower of arrows, plants its feet firmly with dignity.
ai.translation: Those of strong will do not lose heart even in times of ruin; they are like a war-elephant that stands firm with dignity even when pierced by a shower of arrows.
ai.modern: அழிவு வந்த காலத்திலும் மனவலிமை உடையவர்கள் தளர மாட்டார்கள்; அது, அம்புக் கூட்டங்கள் தன் மேல் பட்டுத் துளைத்த போதிலும், தன் பெருமையைக் காக்க கால்களை உறுதியாக ஊன்றி நிற்கும் ஆண் யானையைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares people of strong determination (உரவோர்) to a majestic war-elephant (களிறு). When faced with adversity or ruin (சிதைவிடத்து), these strong-willed individuals do not lose heart or flinch (ஒல்கார்). Just as a battle elephant, even when pierced by a thick shower of arrows (புதையம்பிற் பட்டு), refuses to fall and instead plants its feet firmly to maintain its dignity and strength (பாடு ஊன்றும்), the wise and strong-willed stand resolute against the arrows of misfortune. The key word 'உரவோர்' highlights that true strength is mental, and 'பாடு' emphasizes the dignity maintained during struggle.

ai.literal: Those who lack motivation will not attain in the world the pride called 'we are generous'.
ai.translation: Those who lack inner motivation will never attain the proud joy of saying, 'We are generous,' in this world.
ai.modern: ஊக்கம் இல்லாதவர்கள், 'நாங்கள் கொடைத்தன்மை உடையவர்கள்' என்று பெருமையோடு சொல்லிக்கொள்ளும் மகிழ்ச்சியை இவ்வுலகில் அடையமாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that inner motivation or resolve (உள்ளம்) is the foundation for all great deeds, including philanthropy. Without this driving energy, a person cannot acquire the means or the spirit to help others. Consequently, they will never experience the righteous pride (செருக்கு) and joy that comes from being known as a generous benefactor (வள்ளியம்) in society. The poet uses 'செருக்கு' here not as negative arrogance, but as the healthy self-worth and elation born of noble giving.

ai.literal: Even though it is huge and has sharp tusks, the elephant will fear if a tiger attacks.
ai.translation: Although the elephant is immense in size and armed with sharp tusks, it will tremble in fear if a tiger attacks.
ai.modern: யானை மிகப்பெரிய உடலையும் கூர்மையான தந்தங்களையும் கொண்டிருந்தாலும், ஒரு புலி தன்னைத் தாக்கினால் அது அஞ்சி நடுங்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights that physical size and external weapons are useless without inner courage and determination. The elephant is massive and possesses deadly, sharp tusks, yet it shudders in fear when confronted by a fierce tiger. The tiger, though much smaller, possesses the relentless drive and spirit to attack. For a learner, this teaches that true strength lies in one's inner resolve and motivation, not in outward appearance or resources.

ai.literal: Strength to a person is the wealth of the mind; those who lack that are trees, being different only in being called humans.
ai.translation: A person's true strength is the wealth of their mental energy; those who lack it are like trees, differing only in their human form.
ai.modern: ஒருவருக்கு உண்மையான வலிமை என்பது மன ஊக்கமாகிய செல்வமே ஆகும்; அது இல்லாதவர்கள் மனித வடிவம் பெற்றுள்ளார்கள் என்ற வேறுபாடு மட்டுமே கொண்ட மரங்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines true strength (uram) not as physical power, but as the wealth of inner drive and mental energy (uḷḷa veṟukkai). The poet compares those who lack this inner motivation to inanimate trees (maram). The only difference (vēṟu) between such passive individuals and trees is their outward human appearance (makkaḷ ātalē). Without the active, conscious energy of resolve, a human body is no better than a motionless wooden trunk.
